---
title: "Forcing Transitive Versions via Dependency Management"
tagline: "Or what to do when a transitive dependency is the wrong version"
type: scenario
tool: maven
---

#### ! Scenario

*Or what to do when a transitive dependency is the wrong version*
This scenario demonstrates how to force a specific version of a transitive dependency, overriding what the intermediate libraries request.

::: {.callout-note title="Tool Versions"}
This scenario was tested with **Maven 3.9**; the behaviour shown applies to Maven 3.x.
:::

#### ! Example

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 4.4
graph LR
    Root[Project Root] --> LibA[lib-a:1.0.0]
    LibA --> LibB[lib-b:1.0.0]
    LibB --> LibC[lib-c:1.0.0]
    Root -- manages --> LibC_Forced[lib-c:2.0.0]
```

```{.xml include="pom.xml" snippet="s6-deps"}
```

#### ! Expect
"I said use 2.0.0, so use 2.0.0."

#### ! Actual
Using `<dependencyManagement>`, `lib-c` becomes `2.0.0`: `lib-c-2.0.0.jar` is on the classpath, and `-Dverbose` shows the `1.0.0` that `lib-b` asked for being managed away.

#### ! Why
This scenario uses the exact same `<dependencyManagement>` mechanism as [MS3](../scenario-3-mgmt/guide.qmd), but applies it to a *transitive* dependency instead of a direct one. There is no special "forcing" keyword in Maven. As the resolver collects the graph and reads `lib-b`'s POM, it checks each dependency it finds against the managed set and replaces the requested version with the managed one before going any deeper. The managed version therefore takes effect before nearest-wins ever has two candidates to choose between.

#### ! Fix
This is often the fix when nearest-wins picks an old version, or to patch a vulnerability deep in the graph.

#### ! Risk

* LOW Forcing a version to align with a BOM or to patch a known vulnerability. This is a primary use case for this feature.
* MEDIUM Forcing a version to a newer version that has not been tested with the libraries that depend on it. This can lead to `NoSuchMethodError` if the new version has breaking changes.
* HIGH Forcing a version to an older version. This is very likely to cause problems, as the libraries that depend on it may be using features only available in the newer version.

#### ! Control
This is a safe and recommended pattern for enforcing policy.

#### ! Check

**Fast check:**

```bash
mvn dependency:tree -Dverbose
```

**What to look for:**
`lib-c:jar:2.0.0:compile (version managed from 1.0.0)` under `lib-b`. Without `-Dverbose` you see only the winning `2.0.0`.

**Conclusion:**
A version in `<dependencyManagement>` overrides any transitive dependency version.

#### ! Scales
Managed versions are the usual way security policy reaches the whole graph: "every module must use `jackson-databind` ≥ the patched release" is one `<dependencyManagement>` entry in the parent POM.

#### ! Takeaway
`<dependencyManagement>` overrides transitive version resolution (nearest-wins), making it the primary tool for enforcing version policy across the dependency tree. A direct version in `<dependencies>` still takes precedence ([MS4](../scenario-4-override/guide.qmd)).

#### ! Wild
When Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) was disclosed in December 2021, the question in every Java shop was not "do we declare log4j-core?" but "does anything we depend on declare it?". Most of the exposure was transitive. The fastest safe fix in Maven projects was exactly this scenario: one `<dependencyManagement>` entry pinning `log4j-core` to `2.17.x` in the corporate parent POM, which overrode every transitive request in every module without touching any of them.
